title: Ki Teitzei: build the railing (Deuteronomy 22:8)
hookLine: a new house needs a parapet so no one falls

cards: Houses in ancient Israel had flat roofs, and people used them. They dried flax up there, slept there on hot nights, ate there, talked there. In the Bible, Rahab hides the spies under flax on her roof.

A roof was a room without walls. Which meant that on any warm evening, someone, a child chasing a ball, a guest who'd had a little wine, an old man stepping back to see the stars, was one step from a fall.
One sentence in Ki Teitzei is about that step.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: "When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a parapet for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thy house, if any man fall from thence."
The Hebrew for parapet is ma'akeh: a low wall, a railing. Notice what it asks. Not that you push no one off the roof.

teach.h: A FALL THAT HASN'T HAPPENED YET.
teach.b: It asks you to think ahead about a fall that hasn't happened, to someone you may not even know yet. And if you don't, and someone falls, the verse says the blood is on your house. Not on fate.
On the builder who could have seen it coming. The rabbis ran with it.

teach.h: THE DOG, THE LADDER, THE PIT.
teach.b: The Talmud, in Bava Kamma, says a person shouldn't keep a dangerous dog in the house, or leave a rickety ladder standing, because of this verse.
Maimonides writes that anything on your property that puts life in danger, an open pit, an uncovered well, a weak wall, has to be fixed, and this is both a positive command and a prohibition.
The roof became a stand-in for every hazard you own. Plenty of laws deal with harm after it's done.
This one makes prevention the commandment: caring for other people includes the dull work of thinking about what could go wrong in your own space, and fixing it before anyone gets hurt.

how: Jewish law treats the railing as a real obligation: observant Jews put a parapet around a flat roof or balcony that people use, some say a blessing when building one, and the commandment is cited for home and workplace safety more broadly.

games.q: you've just built a house with a flat roof. no one has ever fallen. what does the Torah say to do?
o: wait and see if it's a problem.
build a railing around the roof.
tell people to be careful up there.
games.why: thou shalt make a parapet for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thy house.

practice: Walk through your home in your mind, room by room, the way a visitor might: the rug that slides, the stairs with no light, the cord across the floor, the smoke alarm with a dead battery.
Go slowly, and let the one most likely to hurt someone come to the front. Picture the railing that hazard needs.
